title: Freedom on Demand
text:
The rise of platform work has promised workers unprecedented flexibility, allowing them to choose when and where they labour. In practice, however, many of these contractors lack the protections traditionally attached to employment, such as sick pay and pension contributions. Their earnings are often precarious, fluctuating with algorithmic demand that the workers themselves cannot predict. Consequently, the boundary between independence and dependence has become increasingly blurred.

Regulators have struggled to classify these workers, since existing legislation was designed for a world of fixed hours and single employers. Some governments have responded by creating an intermediate legal category that grants limited rights without full employee status. Trade unions, meanwhile, argue that collective bargaining is essential to offset the imbalance of power between platforms and individuals. Whether the flexibility on offer will ultimately benefit workers remains a matter of heated debate.

questions.text: According to the first paragraph, what protections do many platform contractors lack?
options: Protections such as sick pay and pension contributions
The right to choose their working hours

questions.text: What have some governments done, according to the second paragraph?
options: Created an intermediate legal category with limited rights
Granted full employee status to every contractor

questions.text: What does the author imply about the flexibility promised by platform work?
options: It has fully delivered on its promises
Its benefits may not be shared equally by workers
It applies only to employees with fixed hours

questions.text: What can be inferred about the role of trade unions in the passage?
options: They oppose any form of regulation
They see collective action as a way to balance power
They have no influence over platforms
They support the abolition of contractor status

paragraph_translations: El auge del trabajo en plataformas ha prometido a los trabajadores una flexibilidad sin precedentes, que les permite elegir cuándo y dónde trabajar. En la práctica, sin embargo, muchos de estos contratistas carecen de las protecciones que tradicionalmente acompañan al empleo, como el pago por enfermedad y las aportaciones a la pensión. Sus ingresos suelen ser precarios, pues fluctúan según una demanda algorítmica que los propios trabajadores no pueden predecir. En consecuencia, la frontera entre independencia y dependencia se ha vuelto cada vez más difusa.

Los reguladores han tenido dificultades para clasificar a estos trabajadores, ya que la legislación vigente se diseñó para un mundo de horarios fijos y de un único empleador. Algunos gobiernos han respondido creando una categoría jurídica intermedia que otorga derechos limitados sin llegar al estatus pleno de empleado. Los sindicatos, por su parte, sostienen que la negociación colectiva es esencial para compensar el desequilibrio de poder entre las plataformas y las personas. Si la flexibilidad que se ofrece beneficiará finalmente a los trabajadores sigue siendo un tema de intenso debate.
